name: Trabzon
summary:
Trabzon (historically Trebizond) is a city on the Black Sea coast of northeastern Turkey and the capital of Trabzon Province. Founded as Trapezous in 756 BCE by Greek colonists from Sinope, it is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the Black Sea region. The ancient city name refers to the table-shaped plateau (trapeza) on which the Greek colony was established.

Trabzon's greatest historical period was the Empire of Trebizond (1204–1461 CE), a Byzantine successor state founded by Alexios I Komnenos after Constantinople fell to the Fourth Crusade. For 257 years, Trebizond maintained independence as the last Byzantine-tradition state in the region, known for its trade wealth from the Silk Road terminus and for the beauty of its court culture. The Hagia Sophia of Trebizond — a 13th-century Byzantine church with remarkable frescoes — is among the finest surviving examples of Byzantine architecture outside Istanbul.

Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II captured Trebizond in 1461 — the final act in eliminating all Byzantine successor states. The city was a major commercial center in the Ottoman Empire, at the head of trade routes connecting the Black Sea to Persia and Central Asia. During World War I, Trabzon was the site of the mass killing of Armenian and Greek Orthodox populations during the Ottoman genocides. It remains a significant city in modern Turkey with a distinctive Laz and Black Sea Greek cultural heritage.
